explanations.text:
●  you ask for something                                       ([main](compiler/cli/human/__init__.py:main))
  │     You type:   human map decompiler.py --text flow.txt
  │     The tool keeps three things: the command "map", the path
  │     to the code file decompiler.py, and the path to flow.txt —
  │     the file where the abstraction sits.
  │     That step lives in the file beside this one.
  │
  ●  the tool finds the pieces of the file               ([block_spans](block_spans))
  │     It reads the file top to bottom and notes every named piece.
  │     A piece is a part of the file that carries its own name,
  │     the way a chapter of a book carries a title.
  │     For each piece the tool notes where it starts and where it stops.
  │     It does this for one reason only: so the abstraction later
  │     must point at a real piece, and cannot point anywhere it likes.
  │
  ●  the tool checks every pin in the abstraction      ([build_anchors](build_anchors))
  │     A pin ties a few words of the abstraction to one piece
  │     of the code file. It looks like this:
  │
  │         [the start](find_root)
  │
  │     the words "the start", pinned to the piece called find_root.
  │     A pin can also name another file of the project, or a piece
  │     of that file, or point into an earlier abstraction instead.
  │     The tool takes the pins one by one and checks three things:
  │         the piece or the file it names is really there
  │         its words appear only once in the abstraction
  │         the earlier abstraction it points into really exists
  │     One bad pin stops the run, and the tool says which check failed.
  │     Nobody is asked and nothing is guessed. The run is instant.
  │
  ●  the abstraction is saved                    ([the map command's own file](compiler/cli/human/cmd_map.py))
        That step lives in the file beside this one. It picks up
        the record of what is abstracted already, numbers the new
        abstraction, ties it to its exact lines, and writes it all
        back. This file only lends it the shared steps above.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  when your code changes                                   ([cmd_sync](cmd_sync))
     The old abstractions now point at the wrong lines, because the
     lines moved. The tool holds the old file next to the new one,
     sees where each line went, and carries every abstraction and
     every pin to its new place. When the change touches no
     abstraction, it saves the mended pins and stops right there.
     Otherwise it asks claude for one thing only: mend the words the
     change made untrue.

       claude answers ──▶ the tool checks every pin ──▶ kept
                               │
                          one is wrong
                               ╰──▶ ask again, and say which
                                    rule broke   (four tries)

  when you reword one abstraction under another        ([repair_stale](repair_stale))
     One abstraction can stand on another: a simpler telling that
     points into a more detailed one. When you reword the detailed
     one, the tool marks the simpler one stale and waits.
     On your word, claude reads the old words and the new words,
     and mends only the sentences that went wrong.

  other things you can ask for                             ([cmd_show](cmd_show))
     show     every abstraction, a warning for each pin that no
              longer fits, for each imported neighbour file with
              no pin to it, for each line of words that two files
              of the project both use, and how much of the file is
              left
     lines    the file with a number in front of every line
     retext   new words for one abstraction
     undo     take the last abstraction back

The tool first looks at the end of the file's name,
  because each kind of file names its pieces its own way.

  A code file, ending in .py:
      a piece is a part of the code with a name of its own —
      a function definition, or a class.
      The tool does not read the code by itself. It hands the
      file to a library: a ready-made helper that ships with
      the language. The library looks at the code without
      running it, and it knows the grammar of the language,
      so it finds every function and every class, where each
      one starts, where it ends, and what sits inside what.
      That is why the pieces are exact, never guessed.
      A file the library cannot read gives no pieces.

  A document, ending in .md:
      a piece is a section under a heading.
      It runs until the next heading of its rank or higher.
      A heading inside a [fenced example](md_spans) does not count.
      Two headings with the same words are refused,
      because a name must hold one thing only.

  A web page, ending in .html:
      the pieces come from two places.
      A tag that appears one time only — head, style, body —
      is a piece, from where it opens to where it closes.
      And every named function inside a script is a piece,
      the nested ones too, found by counting the braces
      that open and close around them.
      A function that carries the name of a tag is refused.

  Any other kind of file gives no pieces at all.

A document can hold an example: a stretch of text shown
  exactly as it is, the way a book quotes a letter.
  A fence marks it: a line of three marks — ``` or ~~~ —
  opens the example, and the same line of marks closes it.

  Inside the fences, nothing is really said — it is only
  shown. A line in there that looks like a heading is just
  a picture of a heading. So the tool passes over it: it
  does not become a piece, and it does not end the section
  it sits in.

  The tool reads the document line by line. At an opening
  fence it stops taking headings, and at the closing fence
  it takes them again.
